title: Toward sustainable and resilient fisheries management for the Humboldt squid deep-water fishery
text:
Introduction
Here we describe the data sources and exploratory data analysis for the project, Toward sustainable and resilient fisheries management for the Humboldt squid deep-water fishery. The project is a collaboration between UCSB’s Environmental Markets Lab (emLab) and Environmental Defense Fund (EDF).

title: Toward sustainable and resilient fisheries management for the Humboldt squid deep-water fishery
text:
Use of generative AI
Claude (Anthropic), model Opus 5.5, was used as a coding assistant through Claude Code in November 2026. It helped move the AIS data to Global Fishing Watch’s V5 pipeline, extend the data through 2025, split the data pipeline into separate projects for the GFW, SST, and analysis steps, switch the SST download to NOAA’s NCEI archive, read the CMIP6 forecasts from the IPCC Atlas dataset, and revise the text and figures in this book.

title: 1  Dataset descriptions
text:
1.1 Sea surface temperature (SST)
Sea surface temperature (SST) data come from NOAA’s daily Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature (OISST) version 2.1 (Huang et al. (2021)). We download the final (not preliminary) daily files from NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) archive, and check that each file holds the expected date before using it. The raw data are provided globally at 0.25x0.25 degree daily resolution. We keep the pixels within the geographic analysis scope (see below), and temporally aggregate the daily data to monthly resolution by calculating the mean (and standard deviation, minimum, and maximum) SST for each pixel from across the days in each month. Every day from 2016-01-01 through 2025-12-31 is included.

title: 1  Dataset descriptions
text:
1.2 Oceanic Niño Index (ONI)
Monthly Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) values come from NOAA’s Physical Sciences Laboratory. The ONI is NOAA’s primary index of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO): the 3-month running mean of sea surface temperature anomalies in the Niño 3.4 region (5°N-5°S, 120°-170°W), from NOAA’s Extended Reconstructed SST (ERSST) dataset. Values of +0.5°C or higher indicate El Niño conditions, and -0.5°C or lower indicate La Niña conditions. NOAA revises past ONI values when it updates ERSST or the index’s base periods, so values for earlier months can shift slightly between data pulls. To keep the analysis reproducible, we use a copy of the ONI file saved on 2026-11-02, and use the ONI for each month from 2016-01-01 through 2025-12-31.

title: 1  Dataset descriptions
section: 1.3 Sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts under climate change
text:
1.3 Sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts under climate change
We use SST forecasts under climate change from the IPCC WGI Interactive Atlas(Iturbide et al. (2021)). The Atlas provides a platform for accessing ensemble forecasts from CMIP6 (Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6), which represent the latest global climate forecasts available and served as the basis of the 6th IPCC Assessment Report.
We use the data underlying the Atlas, the IPCC-WGI AR6 Interactive Atlas Dataset (Instituto de Física de Cantabria, Version 2 final), which has monthly SST from each CMIP6 model interpolated to a common 1x1 degree grid. We read it from the dataset’s THREDDS server, for the 1x1 degree cells within the geographic analysis scope. For each scenario and time horizon, we calculate each model’s mean SST for each calendar month across the years of the time horizon it has data for, then average across the models with SST in each cell. This follows the Atlas’s own code (datasets-interactive-atlas/04_map_figures.R in Iturbide et al. (2021)), and reproduces the values on the Interactive Atlas to within 0.02°C. A few model runs don’t cover every year (e.g., the CAMS-CSM1-0 and IITM-ESM runs end before 2100, and EC-Earth3-Veg-LR is listed for SSP5-8.5 but has no SST data, so SSP5-8.5 means use 26 models); the models and years used are listed in cmip6_models_used.csv in the pipeline outputs. We use three time horizons:

Near Term (2021-2040)
Medium Term (2041-2060)
Long Term (2081-2100)

And for each time horizon, four climate change scenarios (more information on the scenarios can be found here), each with the models the Atlas uses for it:

SSP1-2.6 (26 models)
SSP2-4.5 (28 models)
SSP3-7.0 (24 models)
SSP5-8.5 (27 models)

This gives us a total of 12 different forecasts to analyze. The pipeline checks that each has all 12 months, and that no two are identical. (Until November 2026, we downloaded these forecasts by hand from the Interactive Atlas website. Some of those files turned out to be copies of a different scenario or time horizon, and the Near Term files had no February.) The dataset can be loaded in targets using targets::tar_load(sst_cc_forecast_data), and it has the following columns:

lon_bin: 1x1 degree longitude bin, lower-left corner (degrees) (numeric)

lat_bin: 1x1 degree latitude bin, lower-left corner (degrees) (numeric)

sst_deg_c_mean: Multi-model mean sea surface temperature for the calendar month (degrees C) (numeric)
time_period: Future time horizon forecast time period (character)
scenario: Climate change scenario (character)
month_number: Month number (numeric)

title: 1  Dataset descriptions
text:
1.4 AIS-based fishing effort
We use satellite-based individual vessel monitoring AIS data processed by Global Fishing Watch (Kroodsma et al. (2018)). We use the V5 pipeline table global-fishing-watch.pipe_ais_v5_published.messages. Variables of interest within this table include the following (descriptions are taken directly from the schema for pipe_ais_v5_published.messages):

ssvid: source specific vessel id; MMSI for AIS
hours: time since the previous position in the segment
timestamp: timestamp for position
lon: longitude
lat: latitude
night_loitering: 1 if the seg_id of every message of a squid_jigger that is at night and not moving, 0 if not.

In order to minimize noisy data, we only include AIS messages that have a clean_segs boolean (i.e., all messages must have good_seg boolean and must not have an overlapping_and_short boolean). We filter to just those messages where night_loitering = 1. For squid jigging vessels, GFW uses the heuristic of night loitering to identify when they are fishing. Therefore, any hours where night_loitering = 1 can be classified as fishing_hours
We take the raw high-resolution AIS data and aggregate fishing_hours spatially (by 0.25x0.25 degree pixels, which are roughly 27.75km x 27.75km at the equator), temporally by month, and by flag. We currently process data from 2016-01-01 through 2025-12-31.

title: 1  Dataset descriptions
text:
1.5 AIS-based vessel info
Vessel characteristics data processed are by Global Fishing Watch (Park et al. (2023)). We use the V5 pipeline table global-fishing-watch.pipe_ais_identity_v5_partners_published.vi_ssvid, which has one row per vessel summarizing its whole AIS record. In V5, vessel class, whether a vessel is a fishing vessel, and engine power come from GFW’s random forest vessel classification model (random_forest_info), which replaces the V3 fields best.best_vessel_class and on_fishing_list_best (GFW Pipe5 Release Notes for Research Partners, September 2026). Variables of interest within this table include the following (descriptions of the random_forest_info fields are from the release notes, since the schema does not describe them; the others are taken directly from the schema):

ssvid: source specific vessel id; MMSI for AIS
best.best_flag: best flag state (ISO3) for the vessel
random_forest_info.on_fishing_list_best: whether the vessel is a fishing vessel, from the random forest model, overridden by official registry information where available
random_forest_info.best_vessel_class: best vessel class for the vessel from the random forest model. The model only names a specific gear when it scores that gear at least 0.35; otherwise it rolls the vessel up to a broader class, such as the generic fishing
random_forest_info.atomic_class: the random forest model’s finest-level vessel class prediction
random_forest_info.best_engine_power_kw: best engine power (kilowatts) for the vessel (using official registry information where available, or the random forest model’s estimate where not available)
activity.active_hours: hours the vessel was broadcasting AIS and moving more than 0.1 knots
activity.offsetting: true if this vessel has been seen with an offset postition at some point between 2012 and 2019
activity.overlap_hours_multinames: the total numbers of hours of overlap between two segments where, over the time period of the two segments that overlap (including the non-overlapping time of the segments), the vessel broadcast two or more normalized name, where each normalized name was bradcast at least 10 or more times. That is a bit complicated, but the goal is to identify overlapping segments where there were likely more than one identity. (this should be 0; if it is > 0, it can be used as a filter to remove potentially erroneous/noisy vessels)

We filter to just those vessels the random forest model calls fishing vessels (random_forest_info.on_fishing_list_best) and squid jiggers. A vessel is a squid jigger when random_forest_info.best_vessel_class = squid_jigger, or when the model rolls the vessel up to the generic fishing class but its finest-level prediction is random_forest_info.atomic_class = squid_jigger (GFW says this finest-level prediction is reliable for squid jiggers). Additionally, to reduce noise, we filter out vessels that broadcast exceedingly infrequently (i.e., activity.active_hours < 24) or are noisy vessels, using GFW’s definition of a noisy vessel (i.e., activity.offsetting or activity.overlap_hours_multinames >= 24). They are simply not reliable and will not provide good effort estimates. This leaves us with 4,212 squid vessels globally.

1.5.1 Joined dataset: SST and AIS-based effort
One version of the final dataset we use for our analysis is a combination of the gridded AIS-based fishing effort data and gridded SST data. We start from every 0.25x0.25 degree pixel and month with SST data within the analysis scope, crossed with every flag that has fishing effort in the analysis scope. We then left join the AIS-based effort onto that grid by pixel, month, and flag, so pixel-months with no effort for a flag have zero effort. Each row in the joined dataset represents flag-level effort in a given pixel and month, with the corresponding SST for that pixel and month, the ONI for that month, and the pixel’s EEZ information.
The joined dataset can be loaded in R using the command targets::tar_load(joined_dataset_ais). The dataset has the following columns:

month: Month (first day of month) (date)
lon_bin: 0.25 degree longitude bin (degrees) (numeric)
lat_bin: 0.25 degree latitude bin (degrees) (numeric)
flag: Fishing vessel flag (ISO3) (character)
sst_deg_c_mean: Mean sea surface temperature, aggregated from the raw daily 0.25x0.25 degree data (degrees C) (numeric). The dataset also has the standard deviation, minimum, and maximum (sst_deg_c_sd, sst_deg_c_min, sst_deg_c_max)
fishing_hours: Total fishing effort across vessels (hours) (numeric)
fishing_kw_hours: Total fishing effort across vessels (kW-hours) (numeric)
oceanic_nino_index: Oceanic Niño Index for the month (degrees C) (numeric)
eez_id, eez_iso3, high_seas: The Marine Regions v12 EEZ (MRGID) the pixel’s centroid falls in, and its sovereign (ISO3), or high_seas (Institute (2023)). Joint regimes and disputed areas are not counted as EEZs, so pixels in them are high_seas
nearest_eez_id, nearest_eez_iso3, nearest_eez_distance_m: The sovereign (Marine Regions sovereign MRGID and ISO3) of the pixel’s EEZ, or for high seas pixels, of the nearest EEZ, and the distance (meters) from the pixel’s centroid to the nearest 200 nautical mile boundary between an EEZ and the high seas

title: 1  Dataset descriptions
text:
1.6 Geographic analysis scope
Our proposed geographic scope encompasses a bounding box with a longitude range from -130 degrees to -70 degrees and a latitude range from -40 degrees to 10 degrees (Figure 1.1; Figure 1.2). This longitude range encompasses band of equatorial fishing effort to the west and the EEZs off the western coast of South America. The latitude range covers the maximum latitude of the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organisation (SPRFMO) and extends beyond the southern latitude where the north-south band of fishing effort is currently concentrated. The bounding box extends beyond where fishing effort is currently concentrated, which means that in our predictions under future climate change scenarios, we could capture shifts of fishing effort beyond it current range.








Figure 1.1: Map of squid jigger fishing effort from 2016 through December 2025, aggregating effort across effort, flags, and time for each pixel. EEZ boundaries from Marine Regions V12 are shown in orange; the SPRFRMO boundary is shown in yellow; the currently proposed analysis scope bounding box is shown as a red outline.













Figure 1.2: Zoomed in map of squid jigger fishing effort from 2016 through December 2025 to the proposed analysis scope, aggregating effort across effort, flags, and time for each pixel. EEZ boundaries from Marine Regions V12 are shown in orange; the SPRFRMO boundary is shown in yellow; the currently proposed analysis scope bounding box is shown as a red outline.

title: 2  Exploratory data analysis
text:
2.1 Sea surface temperature (SST)
Note that all maps are zoomed into the area surrounded by the proposed geographic analysis scope.
We can look at a map of SST, simply looking at the average monthly SST from across the entire January 2016 through December 2025 time series (Figure 2.1).
Figure 2.1: Map of mean sea surface temperature (SST) from across January 2016 through December 2025, using 0.25x0.25 degree pixels.
Aggregating across the mean sea surface temperatures of each pixel, we can calculate the mean sea surface temperature over time within our study scope (Figure 2.2). This allows us to see both seasonal trends and larger trends over time.
Figure 2.2: Time series of monthly mean sea surface temperature (SST) within our study scope.

section: 2.2 Sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts under climate change
text:
2.2 Sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts under climate change
Here we look at a map of mean sea surface temperature (SST) under the four different climate change scenarios, and the three different forecast horizons, and focusing on the area of our analysis scope (Figure 2.3).








Figure 2.3: Map of mean August sea surface temperature (SST) under four different climate change scenarios, and three different forecast horizons. Data are for 1x1 degree pixels.





Here we look at time series of climate change forecasts for monthly average SST for each forecast time horizon and scenario, and focusing on our spatial analysis scope (Figure 2.4). As expected, projected SST is higher for time horizon further into the future, and for more extreme climate change scenarios.








Figure 2.4: Climate change forecasts for monthly average SST for each forecast time horizon and scenario, within our spatial analysis scope

title: 2  Exploratory data analysis
text:
2.3 AIS-based Fishing effort
Here we look at total fishing effort from 2016 through December 2025 within the analysis scope, by flag (Figure 2.5). China has the most fishing effort, with 97.2% of all effort, followed by Taiwan with 0.8%.








Figure 2.5: Total fishing effort, by flag, from 2016 through December 2025 within the analysis scope. The label shows the percentage of total fishing effort that each flag contributes. The top 5 flags are shown individually, with other flags aggregated into ‘Other’.





Next we look at a time series of total monthly AIS-based fishing effort by fishing flag over time within the analysis scope (Figure 2.6). The top 5 flags are shown, with other flags aggregated into ‘Other’.








Figure 2.6: Monthly fishing effort by flag from 2016 through December 2025 within the analysis scope. The top 5 flags are shown individually, with other flags aggregated into ‘Other’.





Next we look at a time series of total annual AIS-based fishing effort by fishing flag over time within the analysis scope (Figure 2.7). The top 5 flags are shown, with other flags aggregated into ‘Other’.








Figure 2.7: Annual fishing effort by flag from 2016 through December 2025 within the analysis scope. The top 5 flags are shown individually, with other flags aggregated into ‘Other’.





Next we can look at the temporal trend of total fishing effort alongside the temporal trend of SST (Figure 2.8).








Figure 2.8: Monthly trends of of a) mean sea surface temperature (SST); and b) total squid jigger fishing effort. Both time series include data from across the entire January 2016 through December 2025 time period, and from only within our spatial analysis scope.





We can also aggregate the effort data by calculating the total effort for each month in each year, allowing us to look at the historic seasonal variation of total effort. We can do so for two regions: the “equatorial” region (latitude -10 to 10) and the “sub-equatorial” region (latitude -40 to -10) (Figure 2.9, Figure 2.10).








Figure 2.9: Historic seasonal variation of monthly total fishing effort for the equatorial region. The distribution for each month shows the spread of total fishing effort from each year in our historic dataset (January 2016 through December 2025) and within our spatial analysis scope.













Figure 2.10: Historic seasonal variation of monthly total fishing effort for the sub-equatorial region. The distribution for each month shows the spread of total fishing effort from each year in our historic dataset (January 2016 through December 2025) and within our spatial analysis scope.





We can also aggregate the SST data by calculating the mean SST for each month in each year, allowing us to look at the historic seasonal variation of monthly mean sea surface temperature. We can do so for two regions: the “equatorial” region (latitude -10 to 10) and the “sub-equatorial” region (latitude -40 to -10) (Figure 2.11, Figure 2.12).








Figure 2.11: Historic seasonal variation of monthly mean sea surface temperature (SST) for the equatorial region. The distribution for each month shows the spread of mean SST from each year in our historic dataset (January 2016 through December 2025) and within our spatial analysis scope.













Figure 2.12: Historic seasonal variation of monthly mean sea surface temperature (SST) for the sub-equatorial region. The distribution for each month shows the spread of mean SST from each year in our historic dataset (January 2016 through December 2025) and within our spatial analysis scope.





Next we can look at at a map of AIS-based squid fishing effort (Figure 2.13), aggregating effort across effort and flags and time for each pixel across the entire processed time series. EEZ boundaries from Marine Regions v12 are shown in orange (Institute (2023)).








Figure 2.13: Map of squid jigger fishing effort from 2016 through December 2025, aggregating effort across effort, flags, and time for each pixel. EEZ boundaries from Marine Regions V12 are shown in orange; the SPRFMO boundary is shown in yellow.





We can also look at this map of total fishing effort alongside a map of mean SST (Figure 2.14).








Figure 2.14: Maps of a) mean sea surface temperature (SST); and b) total squid jigger fishing effort (EEZ boundaries from Marine Regions V12 are shown in orange; the SPRFMO boundary is shown in yellow). Both maps include data from across the entire January 2016 through December 2025 time period, using 0.25x0.25 degree pixels.

title: Change log
text:
What changed
AIS data. Squid jigger effort and vessel info now come from Global Fishing Watch’s V5 pipeline instead of V3, and run from January 2016 through December 2025 (V3 ran through August 2024). The BigQuery tables are versioned (_v20261102), so the V3 tables are still there, unchanged. For 2016-2023, V5 has 13.4% more fishing hours and 9.6% more fishing kW-hours than V3 within the analysis scope; the difference is similar every year (9-17% more hours). The squid vessel list has 4,212 vessels.
Pipeline structure. The single targets pipeline is now three projects, run in order with Rscript run.R:

gfw builds the AIS tables in BigQuery and exports them, and the VIIRS detections, to parquet files. It needs GFW BigQuery access.
sst downloads daily SST, saves a dated copy of the ONI, and reads the CMIP6 forecasts. It needs internet.
analysis joins everything and renders this book. It only reads files, so it can be rerun without GFW credentials or internet.

The README describes the safeguards: BigQuery tables are never overwritten, each query has a cost cap, the VIIRS tables are frozen, and downloads and joined datasets are checked before they’re used.
SST. Daily SST now comes from NOAA’s NCEI archive instead of the CoastWatch ERDDAP server. The values are identical for days both have, but ERDDAP was missing some days, and when a day was missing, it returned the nearest day instead. Four of the old daily files held the previous day’s data (2021-03-23, 2021-09-07, 2022-10-19, and 2024-03-31), so those months counted one day twice. With NCEI, every day from 2016-01-01 through 2025-12-31 is included. Monthly SST is now only computed for pixels in the analysis scope.
ONI. The pipeline now uses a copy of NOAA’s ONI file saved on 2026-11-02, and won’t re-download it. NOAA revises past ONI values (it moved to ERSST v6 in September 2026): compared to the previous pull, values for 2017-2021 changed by up to 0.26°C, and 59 of those 60 months changed.
CMIP6 forecasts. The SST forecasts now come from the IPCC AR6 Interactive Atlas Dataset, the data behind the Interactive Atlas, instead of files downloaded by hand from the Atlas website. Of the 144 old files, 63 were copies of a different scenario or time horizon (e.g., Near Term SSP1-2.6 and SSP2-4.5 were identical for five months), the Near Term files had no February, and the Long Term files had two Februaries. The new forecasts follow the Atlas’s own code for averaging across years and models, and reproduce the Atlas values to within 0.02°C. The pipeline also saves a 1995-2014 baseline from the historical runs, for each scenario’s models (sst_cc_baseline_data), for computing projected changes.
EEZs. nearest_eez_id is now the Marine Regions sovereign ID for every pixel. Before, pixels in an EEZ had the EEZ’s ID and high seas pixels had the sovereign’s ID, so one country could have several IDs (e.g., Chile had four). The ISO3 columns didn’t change.
Book. New ONI section; updated SST, CMIP6, and joined dataset descriptions; the scope maps in 1  Dataset descriptions now show effort outside the analysis scope; the annual effort figure is now a stacked bar chart through 2025; map captions now say 0.25x0.25 degree pixels; and figure cross-references are fixed.
Software. R 4.5.1, with packages updated to their latest versions (renv.lock), and Quarto 1.11.9.


Things to flag for Kaiwen
These are in Kaiwen’s analysis files (Analysis_forecast_ols.Rmd, Analysis_forecast_poisson.Rmd, and Visualization.Rmd), which aren’t part of the pipeline. Notes at the top of each file describe them. Only the data loading in those files changed: they now read the analysis project’s store.

Forecasts will change. The CMIP6 files the forecasts used were mislabelled (see above), so the models’ forecasts need to be rerun with the new sst_cc_forecast_data.
CMIP6 is biased warm here. The forecasts swap observed SST for absolute CMIP6 SST. Within the analysis scope, Near Term (2021-2040) CMIP6 SST averages 0.76°C warmer than observed SST for 2016-2025 (SSP1-2.6; 5-95% range of -0.48 to 2.67°C across 1x1 degree cells and months), and the 1995-2014 CMIP6 baseline is already 0.29°C warmer than observed 2016-2025 SST. So part of the predicted change is model bias rather than warming. The delta method (observed SST plus the CMIP6 change from the baseline, for the same cell and month) would avoid this; the baseline is now in the pipeline.
Effort change maps understate effort about 7 times. Rows are pixel x month x flag, and the models have no flag term, so every flag in a pixel-month gets the same prediction. Taking the mean by pixel and multiplying by 12 gives a per-flag number; there are 7 flags in scope.
Wrong scenario. In Visualization.Rmd, ols_prediction_SSP1 is built from the SSP2-4.5 predictions, and the maps named _ssp1 use SSP5-8.5.
February and NAs. With no Near Term February in the old files, February predictions were NA, and mean(na.rm = TRUE) and replace_na(0) showed February as no change. NA predictions should stop the script rather than be dropped.
Region split. monthly_diff splits the regions at lat_bin <= -10, but the models split at lat_bin < -10.
Missing file. capture_quantity.csv isn’t in the repo or the project data folder.
Threads. The models use nthreads = 20, so run them in a Slurm job with at least 20 cores.
Visualization.Rmd stops partway through. A call to plot_sst_change() (the SST change map for January-June) leaves out the required title argument, so the script stops there; the chunk after it then can’t find the plot. This was already in the code. Every other chunk ran.



Running Kaiwen’s analysis files with the new data
On 2026-11-02, we ran the three files in order on sequoia (20 cores), with the new pipeline data. Analysis_forecast_ols.Rmd ran in 24 minutes and Analysis_forecast_poisson.Rmd in 19 minutes, both without errors. Visualization.Rmd stopped at the missing title argument (item 9); run with errors allowed, the rest of it ran. The forecasts in those runs still have the issues in items 2-6, so they aren’t results yet.
